# Matarodanajātaka (Ja 317)

**ID:** Ja 317
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Matarodanajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Matarodanajātaka* (Ja 317) is a canonical birth story preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddakanikāya. According to the prose framework edited by V. Fausböll, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana concerning a landowner (*kuṭumbika*) living in Sāvatthī whose brother had died [Fausböll 1883]. Overcome with grief, the landowner ceased bathing and eating and went weeping to the cemetery every morning [Fausböll 1883]. The teaching opens with the verse phrase *Matamataṁ eva rodatha* ("Weep for the dead / Weep for the living") [Fausböll 1883].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to remove sorrow, and the Buddha similarly brought his hearer to peace; upon the exposition of the four truths at the conclusion of the teaching, the bereaved landowner established himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1883]. In the identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the wise instructor of the past who dispelled the grief of the multitude (*nissokakarapaṇḍita*) as himself [Fausböll 1883].

**Sources**
